extracted.intended_audience: judges and patent litigators drafting or using jury instructions in U.S. patent litigation
extracted.subtask_description: Model jury instructions and accompanying practice guidance for use in United States patent trials, covering claim construction, infringement, invalidity defenses, damages, willfulness, and related trial procedures. Designed to be customized (bracketed terms) to case-specific facts.

rubrics_metrics.name: United States Patents — scope and purpose
rubrics_metrics.description: A patent gives the owner the right to exclude others from making, using, offering to sell, or selling the claimed invention within the United States or importing it into the United States; claims are the numbered sentences that define the scope of the patent owner’s exclusive rights.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explains patent application contents (specification, claims), role of Patent Examiner, the concept of prior art, and prosecution history (file wrapper); intended as background instruction to jurors.

rubrics_metrics.name: Presumption of validity and standard of proof for invalidity
rubrics_metrics.description: A patent is presumed to be valid because it was granted by the PTO; that presumption may be overcome only by clear and convincing evidence that a challenged claim is invalid.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practice Note: consider substituting 'clear and convincing' with language such as 'highly probable' to aid juror understanding; clarifies relation to other evidentiary standards (preponderance of the evidence and beyond a reasonable doubt).

rubrics_metrics.name: Burden and standard for proving infringement
rubrics_metrics.description: [The Plaintiff] must prove that [the Defendant] infringes one or more claims of the patent by a preponderance of the evidence (more likely than not).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Jury must compare accused product/method to the patent claims (not to plaintiff’s commercial product).

rubrics_metrics.name: Claim construction — judge's role
rubrics_metrics.description: It is the judge’s job to provide the meaning of any claim language that must be interpreted; the jury must accept and use the meanings the judge gives for both infringement and invalidity determinations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cites Phillips/Markman/Teva and instructs that claim meanings provided by the court control; read stipulations and court constructions to jury.

rubrics_metrics.name: Claim construction — general principle (use same meaning for infringement and invalidity)
rubrics_metrics.description: Each claim must be considered individually, and the jury must use the same claim meaning for both infringement and invalidity determinations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explicit instruction to avoid different meanings across issues; ties claim construction to §§112 and controlling case law.

rubrics_metrics.name: Means-plus-function (35 U.S.C. §112(f)) claim construction
rubrics_metrics.description: When a claim element is in the form of a 'means' or 'step' for performing a function, the claim is construed to cover the structure, material, or acts described in the specification that perform the recited function and equivalents thereof.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Judge determines the recited function and corresponding structure in the specification; Instruction 2.2 should be given when means-plus-function limitations are at issue to avoid jury confusion; cites Mettler-Toledo, JVW, Utah Med., Valmont.

rubrics_metrics.name: Literal infringement — all claim elements
rubrics_metrics.description: A claim is literally infringed only if the accused product/method includes each and every element (or method step) of that claim.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Literal infringement must be determined claim-by-claim; absence of any claim element defeats literal infringement for that claim.

rubrics_metrics.name: Doctrine of equivalents — insubstantial differences
rubrics_metrics.description: A claim is infringed under the doctrine of equivalents only if the accused product/method contains an equivalent component or step for each claimed element that is not literally present; an equivalent is one that is only insubstantially different and performs substantially the same function, in substantially the same way, to achieve substantially the same result.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Requires a factual determination by the jury by a preponderance of the evidence; includes limitations such as prosecution history estoppel and subject matter dedicated to the public (see separate rubrics).

rubrics_metrics.name: Limitations on doctrine of equivalents — prosecution history estoppel
rubrics_metrics.description: Prosecution history estoppel can bar assertion of equivalents for claim scope surrendered during prosecution.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explains prosecution history/file wrapper and that estoppel is a limitation on DOE; practice notes and citations highlight how estoppel operates as a bar or limit.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limitations on doctrine of equivalents — subject matter dedicated to the public
rubrics_metrics.description: Subject matter expressly dedicated to the public by the patent or its prosecution cannot be reclaimed under the doctrine of equivalents.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Serves as a bar when the specification or prosecution history clarifies dedication.

rubrics_metrics.name: Direct infringement — knowledge and intent immaterial
rubrics_metrics.description: Direct infringement does not require knowledge of the patent or intent to infringe; those mental states are immaterial to the question of direct infringement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cites relevant authority and distinguishes direct infringement from willfulness and inducement concerns.

rubrics_metrics.name: Joint infringement / divided infringement
rubrics_metrics.description: Rules and jury instructions govern situations where multiple actors together perform all claim elements; specific standards address when one party can be held responsible for combined actions of multiple parties.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Instructional guidance to distinguish direct joint infringement issues and ensure jury understands legal tests (text references joint infringement instruction sections).

rubrics_metrics.name: Indirect infringement — inducing infringement (§271(b))
rubrics_metrics.description: A party may be liable for induced infringement if it knowingly induced another to infringe and possessed the requisite intent to cause the acts that constitute infringement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practitioners should distinguish induced infringement from contributory infringement and present appropriate jury instructions about intent and knowledge elements.

rubrics_metrics.name: Contributory infringement (§271(c))
rubrics_metrics.description: A party may be liable for contributory infringement if it sells a component especially made or adapted for use in a patented invention, knowing the same to be especially made or adapted for use in an infringement, and not a staple article suitable for substantial noninfringing use.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Includes statutory reference and case law; instructions must explain knowledge and non-staple/non-infringing-use tests.

rubrics_metrics.name: Infringement by supply of components abroad (§271(f)(1) & (f)(2))
rubrics_metrics.description: Liability arises for supplying all or a substantial portion of components of a patented invention to another country for combination abroad (§271(f)(1)) or supplying components especially made or adapted for use in a patented invention abroad (§271(f)(2)).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Instructions distinguish between the two subsections and set forth elements required under each.

rubrics_metrics.name: Infringement by import, sale, offer for sale or use of product made by patented process (§271(g))
rubrics_metrics.description: Acts involving products made by a patented process that are imported, sold, offered for sale, or used in the United States may constitute infringing acts under §271(g).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Jury instructions must explain the process-patent infringement framework and relevant proof.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prior art — definitions (pre-AIA and AIA)
rubrics_metrics.description: Prior art is technical information existing before the relevant cutoff date; under pre-AIA law different subsections of §102 have different cutoff dates, while under the AIA the Cutoff Date is the effective filing date of the claimed invention.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practice Note: refer to 'Cutoff Date' language; may require separate instructions if different asserted claims have different cutoff dates.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prior art considered or not considered by the USPTO
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether a reference was considered by the Patent Examiner during prosecution can affect its evidentiary context but does not necessarily control validity determinations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Model instructions include specific language about how jurors may treat prior-art evidence and distinctions for art submitted or not submitted to the PTO.

rubrics_metrics.name: Person of ordinary skill in the art (PHOSITA)
rubrics_metrics.description: The level of ordinary skill in the art is defined by reference to education, experience, and training generally possessed by workers in the area at the relevant time (pre-AIA: time of invention; AIA: before effective filing date).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: PHOSITA is a factual construct used for obviousness, enablement, written description, and claim interpretation; jury may need instruction to determine that level.

rubrics_metrics.name: Anticipation (novelty) — generally
rubrics_metrics.description: A claim is anticipated if a single prior-art reference or prior act discloses each and every element of the claimed invention such that the claimed invention is not new.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Anticipation is addressed through prior public knowledge, prior public use, printed publication, prior patent, and prior U.S. application; separate pre-AIA and AIA formulations appear in instructions.

rubrics_metrics.name: On-sale bar
rubrics_metrics.description: Sales or offers for sale before the relevant cutoff date can bar patentability under the on-sale provisions of §102 (pre-AIA and applicable AIA rules).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Model instruction subdivides pre-AIA and AIA considerations and includes experimental use exceptions when applicable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Printed publication — what qualifies as prior art
rubrics_metrics.description: A reference is a printed publication prior to the cutoff date if it was sufficiently accessible to persons interested in the art such that it constituted public knowledge.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Instruction provides factors for jurors to consider in determining whether a reference qualifies as a printed publication.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prior patent and prior U.S. application as prior art
rubrics_metrics.description: Earlier patents or U.S. patent applications/publications may qualify as prior art under pre-AIA and AIA statutory provisions and relevant case law.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Model instructions separate pre-AIA and AIA treatments and explain how earlier patent documents can anticipate or render claims obvious.

rubrics_metrics.name: Obviousness — Graham factors and analysis
rubrics_metrics.description: Obviousness is determined using the Graham framework: (1) scope and content of the prior art; (2) differences between the claimed invention and the prior art; (3) level of ordinary skill in the art; and (4) secondary considerations (objective indicia) such as commercial success, long-felt but unsolved needs, failure of others, and copying.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Model instructions explain combining references, reasons to combine, and secondary considerations; cites controlling case law and distinguishes legal and factual questions for the jury.

rubrics_metrics.name: Enablement requirement (35 U.S.C. §112)
rubrics_metrics.description: The specification must enable a person of ordinary skill in the art to make and use the claimed invention without undue experimentation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Instruction addresses factors relevant to undue experimentation and explains enablement as a factual inquiry for the jury.

rubrics_metrics.name: Written-description requirement (35 U.S.C. §112)
rubrics_metrics.description: The specification must contain a written description sufficient to show that the inventor had possession of the claimed invention at the time of filing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Model instructions clarify written-description as distinct from enablement and include guidance on assessing whether the specification demonstrates possession.

rubrics_metrics.name: Invalidity of independent and dependent claims
rubrics_metrics.description: Invalidity must be considered claim-by-claim; dependent claims incorporate all limitations of the claims from which they depend and can be invalid independent of or in light of their parent claims.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Instructions explain how jurors should approach dependent-claim invalidity relative to independent claims.

rubrics_metrics.name: Damages — general principles and types
rubrics_metrics.description: If infringement is found, the jury must determine the amount of damages to reasonably compensate the patent owner; damages may include lost profits, price erosion, cost escalation, convoyed sales, and reasonable royalty.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Model instructions cover dates for when damages begin, standards for proof, and the idea that damages should not be based on hindsight but on the hypothetical negotiation at the relevant time.

rubrics_metrics.name: Lost profits
rubrics_metrics.description: Lost profits are recoverable where the patentee shows the amount of profits it would have made 'but for' the infringement, under established tests (e.g., Panduit-type factors).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Instruction provides framework for proving lost profits, including causation and reasonable probability of sales to the patent owner absent infringement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Price erosion
rubrics_metrics.description: Damages may include price erosion to the extent infringement caused a reduction in the price the patent owner could have obtained for its product.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Model instructions describe this category and the evidence needed to support it.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cost escalation
rubrics_metrics.description: Damages may account for increases in the patentee’s costs attributable to infringement (cost escalation).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Requires proof tying cost increases to the infringer’s conduct.

rubrics_metrics.name: Convoyed sales
rubrics_metrics.description: Damages may include profits from sales of other products that were bought together with the patented product (convoyed sales) when those sales are properly attributable to the patented feature.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Instruction explains when convoyed-sales damages are appropriate and how to apportion value.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reasonable royalty — hypothetical negotiation framework
rubrics_metrics.description: A reasonable royalty is the amount the parties would have agreed upon in a hypothetical negotiation at the time infringement began (the Georgia-Pacific framework and related factors inform the analysis).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Model instructions require apportionment to the patented technology, prohibit hindsight, but allow consideration of what parties would have foreseen; includes subtopics (EMV rule, multiple patents, timing, substitutes, comparable licenses).

rubrics_metrics.name: Reasonable royalty — Entire Market Value Rule (EMV)
rubrics_metrics.description: Generally royalties should be based on the smallest salable unit practicing the patent; the entire market value of a multi-component product may be used only if the patented feature is the sole driver of customer demand or substantially creates the product’s value.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: EMV is a narrow exception; jury must require proof that patented feature was the basis for customer demand.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reasonable royalty — Multiple patents
rubrics_metrics.description: If multiple patents are infringed, the jury may award separate royalties for each patent and should consider the effect of multiple licenses on the hypothetical negotiation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Includes instruction to consider number of licenses needed and economic effects in hypotheticals.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reasonable royalty — Timing
rubrics_metrics.description: Damages are based on the hypothetical negotiation at the relevant time, but jurors may consider facts the parties could have foreseen, including some post-infringement evidence in appropriate circumstances.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evidence such as subsequent licenses, profits, and usage after infringement may be relevant but care should be taken to avoid purely hindsight-based awards.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reasonable royalty — Availability of non-infringing substitutes
rubrics_metrics.description: Jurors may consider the availability and cost of acceptable non-infringing substitutes when determining reasonable royalty.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: An acceptable substitute is a product/method that would not infringe or that is licensed; model cites to cases on the issue.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reasonable royalty — Use of comparable license agreements
rubrics_metrics.description: Comparable licenses may be considered but must be adjusted for technological and economic differences from the hypothetical license between the parties.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Jury should account for differences between actual licenses offered in evidence and the hypothetical negotiation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Doubts resolved against infringer (record-keeping failures)
rubrics_metrics.description: Any doubts about damages caused by the defendant’s failure to keep proper records should be resolved in favor of the plaintiff.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cites Supreme Court authority and Federal Circuit precedent supporting adverse inferences or resolution against the infringer for inadequate records.

rubrics_metrics.name: Standard-Essential Patents (SEPs) and FRAND considerations
rubrics_metrics.description: For SEPs, jurors must be instructed on the patentee’s FRAND commitment, relevant patent-law principles, and only those Georgia-Pacific factors relevant to the case; jurors must be instructed on apportionment of the portion of the standard and the claimed invention.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practice Note stresses limiting Georgia-Pacific factors to relevant ones and instructing on apportionment between patented technology and value added by standardization.

rubrics_metrics.name: Willful infringement — general standard (Halo)
rubrics_metrics.description: Willfulness requires proof by a preponderance of the evidence that the defendant knew of the patent and intentionally infringed at least one asserted claim; behavior such as malicious, wanton, deliberate, or bad-faith conduct may be considered.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Jury must consider totality of circumstances and defendant’s knowledge at the time; courts must not allow a willfulness finding to improperly affect the damages award (post-Halo guidance).

rubrics_metrics.name: Willful infringement — reliance on legal opinion (35 U.S.C. §298)
rubrics_metrics.description: The absence of an opinion of counsel generally may not be used to prove willfulness; if the defendant relies on a competent legal opinion, jurors may consider reasonable reliance as a factor in assessing willfulness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Instruction should be modified depending on whether defendant asserts reliance on counsel; §298 prohibits using failure to obtain counsel’s opinion as evidence of willfulness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of bracketed template language — customizing instructions
rubrics_metrics.description: Model instructions use bracketed terms (e.g., [the Plaintiff], [the Defendant], [claims in dispute], [abbreviated patent number], [[product] [method]]) to facilitate tailorability to case-specific facts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Guides users to find-and-replace bracketed terms and to select among bracketed options to reflect whether the case involves products, methods, means-plus-function terms, AIA vs pre-AIA issues, etc.

rubrics_metrics.name: Practice Notes — non-binding drafting guidance
rubrics_metrics.description: Practice Notes accompany instructions to provide practical guidance based on judges’ and counsel’s experience and are not to be read to jurors as legal instructions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples include shortening block citations for juror comprehension, avoiding superfluous instructions, distinguishing literal vs DOE infringement, and resolving evidentiary standard phrasing for jurors.

rubrics_metrics.name: Trial procedure and evidence rules for jurors
rubrics_metrics.description: Opening statements and closing arguments are not evidence; deposition testimony is treated as testimony; the trial proceeds in phases and jurors must keep an open mind until all evidence is presented.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Model preliminary instructions explain the six phases of trial, witness testimony formats, and the expectation jurors will follow judge’s legal instructions.
